s001.text: In NFHS-4, the twenty fifteen sixteen survey, Bihar's fertility rate was three point four children per woman.

s002.text: In NFHS-6, the twenty twenty-three twenty-four survey, it is two point seven.

s003.text: Bihar is still the highest of all the places surveyed.

s004.text: In thirty of the thirty-five states and union territories in NFHS-6,

s005.text: the rate is at or below two point one, a number demographers call the replacement level.

s006.text: So what is really happening to India's fertility rate?

s007.text: The answer depends on where you live, and the map holds some surprises.

s008.text: Demographers watch one number above all: the total fertility rate, or TFR.

s009.text: It is the average number of children a woman would have by the end of her childbearing years,

s010.text: if she had children at the rates measured in the years just before the survey.

s011.text: So it is a snapshot of the recent past. It is not a count of how many children each family actually has.

s012.text: The magic line is two point one. The United Nations says the replacement level is about two point one children per woman:

s013.text: enough, on average, for a woman to be replaced by a daughter who survives to childbearing age.

s014.text: Stay below that line for long enough,

s015.text: and if nobody moves in from elsewhere, a country's population eventually starts to shrink.

s016.text: One survey below two point one does not mean a population is shrinking. The key words are "long enough".

s017.text: Every figure for India and its states comes from the National Family Health Survey,

s018.text: conducted by the health ministry with the International Institute for Population Sciences.

s019.text: The sixth round, NFHS-6, covered nearly six point eight lakh households. We use its fact sheets, which are provisional.

s020.text: The counts and comparisons are our own arithmetic. We will say so when we go further.

s021.text: Let us follow India's own line. In the first round, in nineteen ninety-two ninety-three, it was three point four.

s022.text: In NFHS-3, in twenty oh-five oh-six, it was two point seven. In NFHS-4, in twenty fifteen sixteen, it was two point two,

s023.text: just above the line. In NFHS-5, in twenty nineteen twenty-one, it fell to two point zero.

s024.text: That was the first NFHS round to put India below two point one.

s025.text: NFHS-6, whose results the health ministry released on twenty-nine May twenty twenty-six, shows two point zero again.

s026.text: India's rate stays below the line. But India is not one number.

s027.text: It has thirty-six states and union territories, and the NFHS-6 release covers thirty-five of them.

s028.text: Manipur is not in the NFHS-6 release. Those thirty-five places live in very different demographic worlds.

s029.text: Here is NFHS-6, state by state. Of the thirty-five places, thirty are at or below two point one.

s030.text: Twenty-eight are below it, and two, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, sit right on the line at two point one.

s031.text: At the bottom, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands read zero point nine,

s032.text: the only place in the survey below one child per woman. Sikkim comes next, at one point zero.

s033.text: A caution on the islands: their figure rests on about two thousand four hundred women, a small sample.

s034.text: At the top, Bihar reads two point seven. Four places follow at two point two:

s035.text: Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Uttar Pradesh, and the island territory of Lakshadweep.

s036.text: Only five places in the survey are above two point one.

s037.text: Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana in the south,

s038.text: and Gujarat, Maharashtra and Goa in the west, all read one point nine or lower.

s039.text: Between the lowest, zero point nine, and the highest, two point seven, the gap is one point eight children per woman.

s040.text: Some places moved a lot between NFHS-5, in twenty nineteen twenty-one, and NFHS-6, in twenty twenty-three twenty-four.

s041.text: Meghalaya fell from two point nine to two point two, the biggest fall in the survey.

s042.text: Back in NFHS-4 it read three point zero, so most of the fall since then came between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6.

s043.text: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands fell from one point three to zero point nine, again a small-sample place.

s044.text: Bihar, still the highest, fell from three point zero to two point seven.

s045.text: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam and Mizoram each fell by zero point three on the printed figures.

s046.text: Those are rounded to one decimal, so read that as about zero point three.

s047.text: Bihar went from three point four, to three point zero, to two point seven.

s048.text: Assam went from two point two, to one point nine, to one point six.

s049.text: Meghalaya, Bihar and Assam were each lower in every round.

s050.text: So what do the lower-fertility places have in common?

s051.text: We tested two things ourselves, using figures in the same NFHS-6 fact sheets. This part is our analysis, not the survey's.

s052.text: First, the share of women aged fifteen to forty-nine with ten or more years of schooling.

s053.text: Second, the share of women aged twenty to twenty-four who were married before eighteen.

s054.text: Across all thirty-five places, where more women had ten or more years of schooling,

s055.text: fertility tends to be lower. The correlation is minus zero point three six.

s056.text: In Kerala, eighty-seven percent of women had ten or more years of schooling,

s057.text: and three percent of women aged twenty to twenty-four were married before eighteen.

s058.text: In Bihar, the figures are thirty-three percent and thirty-five percent.

s059.text: For child marriage, the link is weaker: plus zero point two nine.

s060.text: With only thirty-five places, a link that weak could partly be chance.

s061.text: Next, compare with NFHS-5. On the same thirty-five places, the schooling link was minus zero point five two,

s062.text: and the child marriage link was plus zero point four six. So both links are weaker in NFHS-6.

s063.text: Part of that comes from one small island territory.

s064.text: Lakshadweep, where eleven hundred fifty women were interviewed, is among the highest in schooling and reads two point two on fertility.

s065.text: Leave it out, and the schooling link is minus zero point four six, against minus zero point five zero in NFHS-5.

s066.text: So the link has softened a little. It has not disappeared.

s067.text: A word of caution. This is a pattern, not proof that one thing causes the other.

s068.text: Many other things differ between states, and we did not test them.

s069.text: Here is the twist. Between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5, of the thirty-three places that can be compared, Manipur included,

s070.text: fourteen fell by zero point three or more on the printed figures.

s071.text: None rose by that much. The other nineteen were about the same.

s072.text: Two read slightly higher: Kerala, from one point six to one point eight,

s073.text: and Tamil Nadu, from one point seven to one point eight.

s074.text: NFHS-6 looks different. In sixteen of the thirty-five places, NFHS-6 is higher than NFHS-5.

s075.text: In twelve it is lower, and in seven it is the same.

s076.text: But look closer. In ten of those sixteen,

s077.text: the difference is just zero point one, and we treat that as about the same.

s078.text: On the printed figures, six places are zero point three or more higher,

s079.text: and six are zero point three or more lower.

s080.text: Among places with bigger samples, the largest rise is Jammu and Kashmir: one point four in NFHS-5, one point eight in NFHS-6.

s081.text: Nagaland fell by a full child per woman between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5, from two point seven to one point seven.

s082.text: In NFHS-6 it reads two point zero, about zero point three higher.

s083.text: A few small places also show jumps,

s084.text: but their samples run from about eight hundred to two thousand two hundred women, so we leave them out.

s085.text: Kerala reads one point eight again, and Tamil Nadu one point seven. Both are about the same.

s086.text: So is India's fall levelling off? One survey cannot tell us.

s087.text: The NFHS-6 numbers are provisional, and only a later survey can show

s088.text: whether this is a turn or just noise.

s089.text: Why does this matter? The United Nations notes that in countries below replacement level, population ageing speeds up.

s090.text: And if fertility keeps falling, then over the long run the share of people of working age shrinks,

s091.text: and the share of older people grows.

s092.text: NFHS-6 already shows different age profiles. In Kerala, twenty point seven percent of people are sixty or older.

s093.text: In Bihar, eleven point five percent. For India as a whole, twelve point nine percent.

s094.text: At the other end, thirty-five point six percent of people in Bihar are under fifteen, against twenty point three percent in Kerala.

s095.text: The table shows how much, not why.

s096.text: So where does your state sit on the map,

s097.text: and what do you see in your own family? Tell us in the comments.

s098.text: There is a new India map on Data Kadai to look at next.
